Parasitic infections in wild-caught Yellow-nosed cotton rats (Sigmodon ochrognathus) from the Chiricahua Mountains have provided data on the growth trajectories of these cricetid rodents. Neonates are born extremely altricial, weighing just 7.3 grams [Wwb = 7.3 grams] at parturition. This modest neonatal mass is typical of the genus Sigmodon. Field observations over several consecutive trapping seasons revealed that adult individuals eventually reach a maximum asymptotic body mass of approximately 120 grams [Wwi = approximately 120 grams]. This final ultimate mass appears to be constrained by local forage quality and is considerably lower than that recorded for the congeneric hispid cotton rat, Sigmodon hispidus, which can exceed 200 grams in more mestic environments. Juveniles grow rapidly during the first weeks of life, with nursing pups doubling their birth weight within the first ten days post-partum.

The timing of early life history transitions in Sigmodon ochrognathus appears tightly linked to the species’ relatively slow life-history pace for a small rodent. At the typical body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], weaning of the altricial pups occurs at 15 days since birth [tx = 15 days since birth]. This relatively short nursing period is characteristic of many sigmodontine rodents, allowing females to rapidly return to breeding condition. Following weaning, the young enter a distinct juvenile stage during which they continue to develop and accumulate somatic mass. They do not, however, achieve sexual maturity until considerably later. Puberty, defined here as the onset of spermatogenesis in males and the first estrus in females, is attained at approximately 45 days since birth [tp = approximately 45 days since birth] when maintained at a core temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This interval between weaning and gonadal maturation suggests a period of necessary somatic growth before reproductive capacity is achieved.

Gestation in the Yellow-nosed cotton rat lasts a total of 34 days [tg = 34 days] when the gravid female maintains her typical body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This gestation period is notably longer than that of many other small-bodied murid rodents, which frequently complete pregnancy in under 25 days, and likely reflects the relatively large size of the full-term litters. Upon parturition, female Sigmodon ochrognathus produce litters that range in size from 2 to 6 pups [N_R_i = litters that range in size from 2 to 6 pups]. The number of offspring per litter appears to vary with maternal body condition and local resource availability, with females in better condition typically producing larger litters. The gestation period itself is a critical interval during which the gestating embryos undergo rapid organogenesis and significant mass accumulation, as the neonatal mass of 7.3 grams represents a substantial investment relative to maternal size.

Reproductive output in this species is driven by a combination of moderate litter size and relatively frequent breeding attempts throughout the favorable season. Female Sigmodon ochrognathus are capable of producing a maximum of approximately 4 to 5 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 4 to 5 litters per year], a remarkably high frequency for a rodent of this size class. This rapid cycling is enabled by the short gestation period and the early weaning of young. When individuals are maintained at their normal active body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], the potential annual productivity is substantial. Combining the average litter size of 4 pups with the maximum litter frequency yields an estimated annual output approaching 24 offspring per female under optimal conditions. This high reproductive potential is characteristic of early-successional grassland rodents that experience high extrinsic mortality rates, favoring a strategy of rapid, repeated breeding over prolonged individual survival.

Maximum longevity in the Yellow-nosed cotton rat has been estimated through mark-recapture studies and comparisons with its well-studied congener, Sigmodon hispidus. The oldest wild individuals are thought to survive for 5.2 years [am = 5.2 years], assuming the species operates at a typical body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This lifespan estimate aligns with expectations for a small mammal with a moderately paced life history; it is shorter than that of many larger-bodied rodents but longer than the average lifespan of some microtine voles. Over this lifespan, an individual female can potentially produce dozens of offspring across multiple breeding seasons. The trade-off between frequent, high-investment reproduction and a relatively constrained lifespan is a central theme in the life-history ecology of this species, and future work should examine how environmental stochasticity and food availability modulate these demographic parameters.
